## Lab 07 Assignment - Group 20

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(broom)  # devtools::install_github("tidymodels/broom")
library(cowplot)
library(ggplot2) 
library(factoextra)
```

```{r}
biopsy <- read_csv("https://wilkelab.org/classes/SDS348/data_sets/biopsy.csv")
```

```{r}
pca_fit <- biopsy %>% 
  select(where(is.numeric)) %>% # retain only numeric columns
  prcomp(scale = TRUE) # do PCA on scaled data

pca_fit
```

```{r}
pca_fit <- biopsy %>% 
  select(where(is.numeric)) %>% # retain only numeric columns
  scale() %>% # scale data
  prcomp() # do PCA

pca_fit
```

## PLOT 1 - Maria

```{r}
pca_fit |>
  broom::augment(biopsy) |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = .fittedPC1,
    y = .fittedPC2,
    color = clump_thickness
  )) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5, alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(
    x = "PC1",
    y = "PC2",
    color = "Clump thickness"
  ) +
  theme_half_open(12) +
  background_grid()
```

## PLOT 2 - Dimitra

### Correlation Matrix of the Biopsy Variables

Before running PCA, visualizing the correlation matrix of the variables, using the ggcorrplot, will check if the variables are related to each other. Only the lower triangle is shown because the matrix is symmetric and similar variables are grouped together.

```{r}
library(ggcorrplot)

biopsy_data <- biopsy |> 
  select(where(is.numeric))

corr_matrix <- cor(biopsy_data)

ggcorrplot(corr_matrix,
           hc.order = TRUE,
           type = "lower",
           lab = TRUE,
           lab_size = 3, 
           title = "Correlation of Biopsy Variables",
           legend.title = "Correlation") +
  labs(caption = "Data from the Wisconsin Breast Cancer Database")
```

### Analysis

All correlations are positive, with the strongest being between uniform cell size and uniform cell shape. This shows that these two variables carry almost the same information. Mitoses has the weakest correlations with all the other variables. This redudancy confirms that PCA is a suitable method for this data.

## PLOT 3 - Joana

### Proportion Plots of Malignancy by Feature Score

This plot represents how the share of malignant tumors changes as each biopsy feature’s score increases from 1 to 10, giving insights of how does every feature is associated with the risk of a tumor being malignant.

```{r}
biopsy |>
  pivot_longer(-outcome, names_to = "feature", values_to = "score") |>
  group_by(feature, score) |>
  summarise(pct_malignant = mean(outcome == "malignant"), n_patients = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  
  ggplot(aes
      (x = score, 
       y = pct_malignant)) +
  geom_line(color = "#8B8682") +
  geom_point(aes(size = n_patients, color = n_patients), alpha = 0.90) +
  scale_color_gradientn(
  colours = c("#FFD700", "#FF7F00", "#EE4000", "#CD0000", "#8B0000"),
  limits = c(100, 500), oob = scales::squish,
  name = "Number of Patients") +
  guides(color = guide_legend(), size = guide_legend()) +
  facet_wrap(~feature) +   
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  
  labs(title = "Percentage of observed malignancy at each score for each feature",
       y = "% malignant", size = "Number of Patients") +
  theme_minimal(11) +
  theme(
    legend.key.size = unit(0.5, "cm"),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 9),
    legend.title = element_text(size = 10)
  )
```

#### Analysis

As we can see, in all nine plots, the percentage of observed malignant tumors generally increases with the score, though the point where we start to see this trend differs by feature, for example for the "mitoses" feature, a low score includes a significant percentage of malignant tumors, but if we look at "clump thickness", this share starts rising at a much higher score. Finally, most patients have low scores, so percentages at high scores are based on few patients.

## PLOT 4 - Leonor

### Principal Component Analysis Biplot

To investigate the multivariate relationships among biopsy samples, we constructed a PCA biplot using the factoextra package. The plot maps the observations onto the first two principal components (PC_1 and PC_2) and displays feature loading vectors to show how each attribute contributes to sample variance. Observations are grouped by diagnostic status (benign vs. malignant) with 95% confidence ellipses.

```{r}
biopsy_clean <- biopsy |> 
  drop_na()

fviz_pca_biplot(
  pca_fit,
  geom.ind = "point",
  col.ind = biopsy_clean$outcome,
  palette = "jco",
  addEllipses = TRUE,
  ellipse.level = 0.95,
  col.var = "black",
  repel = TRUE,
  legend.title = "Outcome"
) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "PCA Plot for Biopsy Data",
       caption = "Plot Design from \nhttps://www.r-bloggers.com/2026/06/pca-in-r-principal-component-analysis-step-by-step-prcomp-ggplot2/#google_vignette",
       subtitle = "Projection of samples and feature loadings onto PC1 and PC2") +
  theme(
    plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 8, color = "gray30")
  )
```

#### Analysis

The PCA biplot clearly separates benign and malignant tumors along PC_1 (65.5% variance). Benign samples cluster tightly on the right, malignant ones spread out on the left. All feature vectors point toward malignant tumors, with most cellular traits driving PC_1 and mitoses standing out along PC_2 (8.6% variance).

## PLOT 5 - Edu

### Ridge Density Plots of all features

```{r}
library(ggridges)
```

```{r}
biopsy |> 
  pivot_longer(cols = -outcome, names_to = "feature", values_to = "value") |> 
  
  ggplot(aes(x = value,
             y = feature,
             fill = outcome)) +
  
  geom_density_ridges(alpha = 0.5) +
  
  theme_ridges() + 
  
  labs(title = "Ridge Density Plots of all features",
       subtitle = "Divided by tumor expression outcome",
       x = "Values (0-10)",
       y = "Feature",
       fill = "Outcome")
```

**Analysis:** It's possible to see that malignant and benign cells are very different.

Some features can even be used as strong predictors of malignancy, like *uniform_cell_size, bare_nuclei,* and *uniform_cell_shape,* as these features exhibit sharp differences between the two possible outcomes.
